terms.grammar: adjective, one ending, with esse; the person or thing outlived in the dative (less often the genitive)
evidence: Cic. N.D. 2.72: ut suī sibi līberī superstitēs essent (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The usual way to say survive: superstes esse alicui, to outlive someone; superstes alone, a survivor. Of things too: a name or a book that lives on (Tacitus, below).

evidence: Caes. BG 1.26: circiter mīlia hominum CXXX superfuērunt
terms.comment: Chiefly to be left over (see remain); of people, to be still alive after others are dead, as Caesar counts the survivors of a battle. Lewis & Short calls the sense rare.
For “survival” as an abstract noun: dē salūte agitur, survival is at stake. Of a person who comes through unharmed, incolumis (Cic. Cat. 3.10 fin., integrōs incolumēsque, Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Agricola posteritātī narrātus et trāditus superstes erit
phrases.english: Agricola, told and handed down to those who come after, will survive

phrases.latin: ut suī sibi līberī superstitēs essent
phrases.english: that their children should outlive them
